headline: High-risk workspace and network overlap: nullclaw can read/write and egress broadly while awesome-nlp is non-runnable, making prompt-injection and leakage pathways mostly one-sided but still operationally risky.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: nullclaw can read/write files, use MCP, browsers, and stdin/stdout, so it can ingest attacker-controlled content from shared channels; awesome-nlp is non-runnable and has no I/O surfaces, so the interaction is mostly one-way. Because the pair lacks a documented bridge, uncertainty remains and I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF nullclaw is configured to ingest files or MCP outputs from a shared workspace, prompt injection becomes reachable.
IF awesome-nlp content is manually copied into nullclaw prompts, instruction hijacking is possible.
mitigations: Disable MCP and browser ingestion for untrusted content.
Keep awesome-nlp artifacts in a read-only directory.
Add a manual review step before any prompt includes repository text.
Use separate workspaces for the two agents.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for all imported text.

B_data_leakage.rationale: nullclaw touches secrets, workspace files, logs, and broad network egress; awesome-nlp has no data surfaces and no network egress. The pair does not show a shared filesystem, but nullclaw's default data handling can leak any copied workspace or secret material once it is fed into its context, so the plausible blast radius is sensitive data.
conditions: IF sensitive files from awesome-nlp are placed into nullclaw's workspace, they can be exposed through logs or outbound requests.
IF nullclaw is connected to external APIs, any imported secrets may leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Do not place secrets in the shared workspace.
Rotate any credentials before testing the pair.
Restrict nullclaw egress to allowlisted endpoints.
Separate repositories and runtime directories.
requires-engineering: enforce content redaction before outbound calls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-nlp is non-runnable and has no write or network capabilities, while nullclaw has broad write, git, and shell authority. There is no overlapping mutable surface shown in the profiles, so direct write-write conflict is not evidenced; the remaining risk is limited to unusual orchestration that forces both onto the same files.
conditions: IF an operator mounts the same writable directory into nullclaw and another writer, file races become possible.
IF awesome-nlp is wrapped by an external runner that writes into nullclaw's workspace, conflicts can occur.
mitigations: Keep awesome-nlp as a static reference only.
Use per-agent directories with distinct ownership.
Avoid concurrent git operations in nullclaw.
Lock shared files before edits.
requires-engineering: add filesystem locking around shared workspaces.

D_cascading_error.rationale: awesome-nlp is an awesome-list, not an executing agent, so it does not generate actions; nullclaw can act on inputs, but the pair lacks evidence that nullclaw treats awesome-nlp output as authoritative by default. That makes cascading error possible only through manual copying or custom orchestration, which is lower risk than default automation.
conditions: IF a user copies repository text from awesome-nlp into nullclaw without verification, nullclaw may act on stale or incorrect facts.
IF nullclaw is scripted to execute tasks from imported text, downstream errors can cascade.
mitigations: Verify any copied facts against primary sources.
Require human approval before nullclaw acts on imported content.
Keep awesome-nlp as a read-only reference.
Disable auto-execution for imported instructions.
requires-engineering: add citation checks before action-taking.

E_compliance.rationale: awesome-nlp is a public open-source list with no touched data classes, while nullclaw handles secrets, logs, workspace files, and broad network egress. No residency or certification mismatch is documented, so only a limited compliance gap exists if regulated data is introduced into nullclaw's broader processing environment.
conditions: IF regulated data is entered into nullclaw, its logging and network surfaces may create retention or residency issues.
IF the deployment requires HIPAA/GDPR controls, nullclaw's documented surfaces must be reviewed before use.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in nullclaw.
Review retention settings before deployment.
Disable unnecessary logging.
Keep public reference material separate from operational data.
requires-engineering: map data flows to residency and retention controls.
